summary:
LunarOps — Where Sunlight Meets Signal:

What if planning a mission to the Moon were as intuitive as exploring a map?

At the lunar South Pole, sunlight is essential for solar-powered operations, while visibility of Earth is critical for direct communication. Rugged terrain and changing celestial positions make finding suitable operational windows a challenging problem.

LunarOps is an interactive 3D lunar exploration and landing-site comparison platform that transforms this complex scientific problem into an accessible visual experience.

Users can explore five example lunar locations, select two sites, choose mission dates, and analyze estimated solar illumination, Earth line-of-sight visibility, terrain obstruction, and overlapping operational windows.

Powered by NASA/JPL DE421 ephemeris data through SpiceyPy, LunarOps integrates real celestial-position calculations with a simplified terrain-horizon model. Our platform transparently identifies which NASA datasets are actively used and which terrain components remain approximations.

Built using Next.js, Three.js, Python/FastAPI, and AWS, LunarOps combines planetary science, interactive visualization, and cloud technology in a publicly accessible application.

Our mission is simple: make lunar exploration easier to understand, compare, and plan—one landing site at a time.
details:
LunarOps is an interactive 3D lunar mission-analysis platform designed to make landing-site exploration and mission planning more intuitive, accessible, and scientifically informed. At the Moon's South Pole, rugged terrain, deep craters, and changing celestial positions create significant challenges for solar-powered operations and direct-to-Earth communication. Understanding where and when sunlight and Earth visibility are available is therefore essential when evaluating potential landing sites. LunarOps addresses this challenge by transforming complex lunar geometry into an immersive visual experience that allows users to explore the Moon, compare candidate locations, and investigate potential operational windows.

Through an interactive 3D environment, users can select two lunar locations from five example sites, choose mission dates and simulation intervals, and generate comparative scientific visualizations. The platform displays estimated sunlight availability, Earth line-of-sight visibility, potential darkness periods, overlapping visibility windows, and terrain-horizon profiles. Interactive dashboards and plain-language explanations help users understand the trade-offs between candidate locations without requiring advanced knowledge of orbital mechanics.

At the core of LunarOps is a Python FastAPI scientific backend that uses NASA/JPL DE421 ephemeris data through SpiceyPy, together with supporting SPICE kernels, to calculate Sun and Earth positions relative to selected lunar locations. These calculations are combined with simplified synthetic terrain-horizon models to estimate local visibility conditions. The platform clearly distinguishes NASA-derived numerical inputs from approximations through its NASA Data Sources interface. Although NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA datasets provide important scientific context, actual LOLA elevation rasters are not yet integrated into the current prototype. Consequently, LunarOps estimates geometric visibility rather than guaranteeing electrical power availability, radio-link reliability, or mission safety.

The application combines Next.js, React, Three.js, and React Three Fiber for its immersive frontend with Python, FastAPI, and SpiceyPy for scientific analysis. It is deployed on Amazon Web Services using Amazon ECS Fargate, Amazon ECR, Amazon CloudFront, an internal Application Load Balancer, and AWS WAF. Terraform provides reproducible infrastructure configuration, while GitHub Actions automates testing, security verification, and cloud deployment. This architecture makes LunarOps a publicly accessible demonstration of how space science, interactive visualization, and modern cloud engineering can work together.

What makes LunarOps distinctive is its combination of real NASA/JPL ephemeris calculations, interactive 3D exploration, intuitive comparison dashboards, and transparent scientific data provenance. Rather than presenting complex astronomical calculations as isolated numerical outputs, LunarOps turns them into an engaging experience that enables users to investigate how different locations and mission dates affect potential visibility conditions. This approach supports scientific education, encourages exploration of open NASA resources, and makes lunar mission-planning concepts easier to communicate to students, educators, researchers, and the wider public.

Looking ahead, LunarOps can evolve through the integration of real NASA LOLA digital elevation models, improved terrain-horizon reconstruction, independent numerical validation, and additional thermal, power, and communication-link analysis. Our long-term vision is to bridge the gap between complex space-science data and accessible exploration tools, helping more people understand the challenges and possibilities of sustainable lunar exploration. The working application is available at https://d3v97h38thw445.cloudfront.net/ and the source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ARWA044/LunarOps.
